actual_action: The 1969 review did not terminate the study; it continued until public exposure and a separate federal review in 1972.
later_evidence: CDC's historical account records that the participants had not provided informed consent and were not offered treatment even after penicillin became widely available.
The study became public through news reporting in 1972, triggering an Ad Hoc Advisory Panel review.
outcomes: The untreated-study design continued for roughly three more years after the 1969 review.
In 1972 the federal advisory panel concluded that the study was ethically unjustified and advised stopping it.
The study ended in 1972; subsequent reforms strengthened human-subject research protections.
later_reviews_or_findings: CDC now explicitly identifies absence of informed consent and withholding of available treatment as reasons the study was unethical.
The case became a major influence on later research-ethics safeguards and trust in public-health institutions.
